title: 'We lost over £1,000': Why some passengers were hit harder than others by air traffic chaos
preview: Flight disruption has ruined holidays and left passengers sleeping on airport floors - so what are their rights?
summary_raw: Flight disruption has ruined holidays and left passengers sleeping on airport floors - so what are their rights?
full_text_clean:
Image caption, Catie and Phil unpacking at home

Cost of living correspondent Published 10 September 2026 Catie and Phil Allen should have been enjoying their first holiday in two-and-a-half years. Instead, they are at home ringing round for refunds that won't be paid.

The couple are among the many thousands of air passengers caught up in the chaos caused by the four-hour shutdown of the UK's air traffic control system on Tuesday.

It means their holiday to Slovenia has been cancelled and - although their flight was refunded by British Airways - they estimate being left £1,300 out of pocket from unused accommodation and excursions.

It's not the first time - and won't be the last - when passengers are left flying on a wing and a prayer after problems at UK airports. So, here is how their case relates to others, and why they have taken such a big hit.

Catie, 30, and Phil, 34, were sat on a British Airways flight to Ljubljana on Tuesday that never took off.

If a flight is cancelled, airlines must get customers to their destination as quickly as possible at no extra cost, even if it is with a rival carrier.

Alternatively, passengers can take a refund, which should also be offered for flight delays of more than five hours.

In Catie and Phil's case, the alternative flight offered would not have arrived until Saturday morning - four days into their week-long holiday.

So they took the refund. That was not easy. The chatbot only seemed to allow them to rebook, and it took more than an hour waiting to speak to BA on the phone before the refund was confirmed. It will take a week to be paid.

When airlines are at fault, extra compensation is paid under UK and EU rules. But not this time, because the air traffic control issues were beyond airlines' control. Even so, airlines themselves are furious that they have been saddled with a bill of millions of pounds.

BA also refunded the couple's car hire, which had been organised through the airline. The problem for the couple was that they had booked accommodation and excursions separately, and that is money they have lost.

The hotel stays, booked separately, have their own terms and conditions and cancelling so late meant there were no refunds. One explained to Catie that they were a family business that could not afford to do so.

This is different to package holidays, which are covered in full if a flight is cancelled.

"We feel we are penalised for trying to save money," said Catie, who contacted BBC Your Voice about their situation, although she added that "our problems are very small in the bigger scheme of things".

Image source, Catie Allen Image caption, Catie and Phil during a happier break

One excursion was later refunded but - having worked in the aviation sector - Catie is annoyed that the air traffic problem extended so long as to ruin their holiday.

"We have been saving tirelessly for this trip and we have lost over £1,000 with no way of getting it back. And most of all, we've got no holiday to go on, which we've been looking forward to for years," she said.

The couple said they have been loyal customers of their insurance company for years, and used them for policies ranging from home insurance to pet cover.

However, the insurer told them any claim on their travel insurance for the funds they have lost would be invalid because air traffic issues were outside of the policy.

Some people also make claims via credit card providers. However, all these depend on the small print from providers.

Although the Allens could get back home after their flight was cancelled, others ended up sleeping on floors at Heathrow Airport.

Delayed passengers must be supplied with food and a hotel stay, depending on the length of the wait.

Should the airline not provide them with this, then claims for reasonable expenses can be made afterwards. Experts suggest people keep receipts as proof.

Image source, Dan Kitwood / Getty Images The trouble was that many couldn't find accommodation anywhere nearby. Booking a luxury stay is unlikely to be refunded by the airline, because only "reasonable expenses" are permitted.

On Thursday, Aviation Minister Keir Mather told MPs: "Passengers may also be entitled to care and assistance while waiting for a delayed or re-routed flight.

"But there are, of course, lots of incidences we have seen of airport capacity not being able to deal with the number of passengers being disrupted and I think that is a key lesson we have to learn from this."

Mather said the kind of disruption cause by the failure of air traffic control provider Nats on Tuesday was "unacceptable".

There will be an independent review of the saga by the Civil Aviation Authority.

Flight data firm Cirium said the aviation system had "stabilised significantly" on Thursday.

It said 54 of 3,028 scheduled arrivals had been cancelled or are not operating, while for departures, 47 of 3,033 scheduled flights were affected.

"We have been saving tirelessly for this trip and we have lost over £1,000 with no way of getting it back. And most of all, we've got no holiday to go on, which we've been looking forward to for years," she said.

The couple said they have been loyal customers of their insurance company for years, and used them for policies ranging from home insurance to pet cover.

However, the insurer told them any claim on their travel insurance for the funds they have lost would be invalid because air traffic issues were outside of the policy.

Some people also make claims via credit card providers. However, all these depend on the small print from providers.

Although the Allens could get back home after their flight was cancelled, others ended up sleeping on floors at Heathrow Airport.

Delayed passengers must be supplied with food and a hotel stay, depending on the length of the wait.

Should the airline not provide them with this, then claims for reasonable expenses can be made afterwards. Experts suggest people keep receipts as proof.

Image source, Dan Kitwood / Getty Images The trouble was that many couldn't find accommodation anywhere nearby. Booking a luxury stay is unlikely to be refunded by the airline, because only "reasonable expenses" are permitted.

On Thursday, Aviation Minister Keir Mather told MPs: "Passengers may also be entitled to care and assistance while waiting for a delayed or re-routed flight.

"But there are, of course, lots of incidences we have seen of airport capacity not being able to deal with the number of passengers being disrupted and I think that is a key lesson we have to learn from this."

Mather said the kind of disruption cause by the failure of air traffic control provider Nats on Tuesday was "unacceptable".

There will be an independent review of the saga by the Civil Aviation Authority.

Flight data firm Cirium said the aviation system had "stabilised significantly" on Thursday.

It said 54 of 3,028 scheduled arrivals had been cancelled or are not operating, while for departures, 47 of 3,033 scheduled flights were affected.

title: One year after Charlie Kirk's death, conservative students struggle to fill void he left
preview: The assassination sent shockwaves through the conservative youth movement, which students say has lost momentum and a vital figurehead.
summary_raw: The assassination sent shockwaves through the conservative youth movement, which students say has lost momentum and a vital figurehead.
full_text_clean:
Image source, Jeb Jacobi Image caption, Jeb Jacobi witnessed Kirk's murder at Utah Valley University

Jeb Jacobi still remembers the echo of the gunshot that killed Charlie Kirk.

He was a volunteer at the Turning Point USA event at Utah Valley University (UVU), where Kirk was set to engage in one of his famous live debates on 10 September last year.

But when the conservative activist collapsed, hit by a bullet fired from a sniper rifle, onlookers like Jacobi say they saw their hero become a martyr right before their eyes.

"It feels like there's a forever stain on us here," the third-year university student tells the BBC, as he reflects on the past year since Kirk's death. "This is where Charlie Kirk was killed."

In the wake of the assassination, Jacobi and many others thought that Turning Point USA (TPUSA), the organisation founded by Kirk, could only grow as Kirk's reputation as a conservative activist spread far and wide.

Now, he says, no-one has been able to fill the void.

"It's not the same organisation," he says. "It just doesn't have the same power, the same impact."

By contrast, one of TPUSA's chapter leaders elsewhere in the US denied any suggestion that the organisation was not what it was under Kirk - telling the BBC "this is quite literally just the beginning".

How a college dropout from the suburbs became Maga star Charlie Kirk

Published 12 September 2025 In the immediate aftermath of Kirk's death, support for TPUSA surged. A spokesperson posted on X five days after the killing that the organisation had received "over 32,000 inquiries in the last 48 hours to start new campus chapters".

Since then, however, many like Jacobi have noted a slowing momentum. There has been infighting between more moderate and right-wing factions within the organisation, current members say. In Arkansas, one chapter completely changed its name to disassociate itself from the Kirk-founded organisation, unhappy with the direction in which students felt it was heading.

The BBC contacted TPUSA for comment for this article, but has not received a response.

Utah Valley is located in a conservative area – where registered Republicans outnumber Democrats more than seven to one. But the shooting and political aftermath triggered a kind of culture war - on and off campus.

Jacobi feels his campus is more divided than ever now.

"The culture has gotten more hostile," he says.

"I love for everyone to have their own viewpoints and [be] sharing them," he adds. "The debate is good for society. It's what Charlie did."

Kirk made a name for himself by hosting debates on college campuses where he would spar with people who opposed his views. His popularity on campuses and online made him a rising star in the Republican Party, and President Donald Trump credited Kirk with helping getting young men to vote for him in the last election.

But critics argued that Kirk's debates were designed purely to stoke outrage and garner social media attention, while promoting misogyny, racism and homophobia.

Since his death, some students at UVU have protested against a campus memorial to the conservative activist. They have also tried to stop an event memorialising him from taking place on Thursday, the anniversary of Kirk's death.

Anthony Shinkle, another UVU student, notes how the school's TPUSA chapter and socialist clubs are often in conflict with each other on campus.

He fears Kirk's shooting, and its politically contentious aftermath, have made some supporters afraid to share their political ideology - and sent others further towards more extreme or fringe positions.

"These are impressionable people, impressionable youth," he said, noting how they watched their political hero "be murdered very, very graphically".

"I feel like the assassin got exactly what he wanted," Shinkle, who turns 21 next month, says. "It really feels like there's not anyone who can fill [Kirk's] shoes."

Earlier this month, a judge in Utah cleared the way for a trial of Tyler Robinson, the man accused of shooting Kirk. Robinson denies aggravated murder, a capital offence in the state, as well as six other charges.

Charlie Kirk murder suspect pleads not guilty as judge clears way for death penalty trial

Published 2 September Jacobi says many people have tried to fill the void left by the 31-year-old activist and father of two.

"Sure, they can echo the conservative message, but they can't do what Charlie did," he says. "He had such a way with his words to draw people in, to make them think, to debate, to get people involved."

"You just don't see that with anyone else," he adds. "I don't know if there will be another him."

Such a dip is not unusual following the assassination of a central founding figure like Kirk, says Mark Brewer, chair of the political science department at the University of Maine.

"You have a movement that was started and led by this kind of charismatic figure, and the charismatic figure goes away," he said. "A little bit of loss of momentum isn't exactly surprising."

He notes that Kirk's "personal status as a martyr remains very strong. You can see plenty of folks on the right who are trying to claim the… affiliation with Kirk."

"In some ways, that maybe has only increased," he said. "Kirk himself, in his own influence of his legacy, I don't think that's going anywhere."

There is, however, "a vacuum", he says.

Image source, Reuters Image caption, Kirk's widow Erika has become CEO of Turning Point USA after her husband's death

Macy Gunnell, 22, started a TPUSA chapter at St Mary's College in Indiana following Kirk's death. She says she had tried for years to start one, but it was only after his death that she got the approval.

Gunnell acknowledges divisions within the organisation - but takes a more optimistic viewpoint.

"While there are flying accusations out there that Turning Point is dead, Turning Point's become something that it never was, Turning Point became everything Charlie hated - that could not be further from the truth," says Gunnell, 22, who has since graduated and works in media in Washington DC.

A debater still affiliated with TPUSA, Gunnell travelled to its headquarters over the summer and met Erika Kirk, the founder's widow who took over as CEO, along with the organisation's spokesman Andrew Kolvet.

"I'm confident that Turning Point's not going anywhere, and this is quite literally just the beginning," she says.

Gunnell is among the speakers featured in TPUSA's new Pick Up the Mic campaign - sending debaters to campuses and high schools across the country to continue Kirk's traditions engaging in the art of rhetoric. It begins this semester.

Back at UVU, Jacobi also hopes and believes TPUSA will still grow. He points to a fellow student who was never interested in politics but, after Kirk's death, now helps run their school's chapter of the group.

"I think it's still building," he says.

Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Many say Kirk became a martyr for his conservative Christian youth movement

The killing of Kirk has shaken Shinkle, whose family in Alabama always told him how much safer Utah would be than his home state.

"I kind of feel a weird sense of guilt," he says. "I feel like it's a common sentiment, that everyone wishes they could have done something."

Jacobi, meanwhile, says he had turned to religion instead of deepening his connections with politics.

"When Charlie died, I took a look at myself," he says. "There are so many people who make politics their entire identity. It's so unhealthy for you."

"It really made me realise I needed and wanted a relationship with Christ like Charlie had," he adds. "Ever since I got more involved, I've felt much happier and more peaceful of a person."

And what happens to Turning Point, Prof Brewer says, remains to be seen.

"The final part of the story hasn't been written yet," he said. "So I think a lot will be determined over the next six, 12, 18 months."

title: Can you make a case for Chelsea being stripped of 2016-17 title?
preview: Does Mauricio Pochettino have a case that Tottenham should be retrospectively crowned Premier League champions?
summary_raw: Does Mauricio Pochettino have a case that Tottenham should be retrospectively crowned Premier League champions?
full_text_clean:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Chelsea signed Eden Hazard from a string of other clubs by paying £5.6m to an unregistered agent

Football issues correspondent Published 10 September 2026 Should Tottenham be retrospectively crowned Premier League champions for the 2016-17 season?

That's the opinion of former manager Mauricio Pochettino, who led Spurs to a second-place finish - seven points behind Chelsea - that season.

This is about Chelsea making £47m in secret payments, according to a Premier League investigation, to unregistered agents and third parties to seal transfers between 2011 and 2018.

The transfers included Eden Hazard, Samuel Eto'o, Willian, Ramires, David Luiz, Andre Schurrle and Nemanja Matic.

Four of those - Hazard, Willian, Luiz and Matic - were at the club in 2016-17.

During that period Chelsea won two Premier League titles (2014-15 and 2016-17), two FA Cups (2011-12 and 2017-18), the EFL Cup (2014-15) and the Europa League (2018–19).

Chelsea have been fined by Uefa, the Premier League and the Football Association, but Pochettino thinks that is not enough.

"If they admitted they broke the rules, the Premier League title was for the second-best team," Pochettino said.

Pochettino is one of the first people of significance to articulate what many feel - that Chelsea got off lightly with a fine.

Fans of Everton and Nottingham Forest have pointed out that their clubs faced points deductions for relatively small profit and sustainability breaches, while Chelsea sought to sign star players with secret payments.

Meanwhile, there is no sign of a verdict in the case of Manchester City's 115 charges for alleged breaches of Premier League financial rules.

Does Pochettino have a point? And how much of an impact did those four players have on the title race?

Hazard is seen as the poster boy for Chelsea 's breaches.

The Blues fought off most of Europe's top clubs to sign him from Lille for £32m in the summer of 2012.

Between May 2013 and August 2016, according to the investigation, seven payments totalling £5.6m were made to an unregistered agent "for the benefit of the club in connection with Hazard's transfer".

Pochettino's argument is that Spurs could have beaten other clubs to the signing of players of similar ability had they also ignored the rules.

What about Hazard's impact in the 2016-17 season?

The Belgium forward started 36 Premier League games, scored 16 goals and provided five assists. Only Cesar Azpilicueta started more matches, and only Diego Costa netted more goals (20).

Hazard was Chelsea 's player of the year, was named in the Professional Footballers' Association (PFA) team of the year, and made the shortlist for PFA player of the year.

Then there's the direct impact of his goals and assists in the results of four fixtures.

Hazard scored the first goal in a 2-1 win over West Ham in August, then scored a goal and provided an assist in a 2-0 victory over Southampton in November.

In March he scored the opener as Chelsea again beat the Hammers 2-1, and got both goals in a 2-0 win over Manchester City in April.

You could argue that input was worth 10 points.

There is no doubt that Hazard had a huge influence, but this was his fifth season at the club. It was not as if Chelsea signed him in the summer of 2016.

Premier League boss explains why Chelsea avoided points deduction

Willian joined Chelsea from Anzhi Makhachkala in 2013, with the investigation finding that transfer fee payments totalling £19.2m were made to two unregistered entities in connection with his move and that of Samuel Eto'o.

Willian was not a regular starter in 2016-17, with 19 of his 34 appearances coming from the bench.

But he still had a huge influence, scoring eight goals and providing eight assists.

The Brazilian's attacking returns were crucial in four matches.

He had an assist in a 1-0 win at Sunderland in December. He scored two goals in a 4-2 victory over Stoke in December, and the first goal as Chelsea beat Stoke 2-1 in March. He provided an assist for the winning goal in a 4-3 victory over Watford in May.

His contributions helped Chelsea take eight points from those fixtures.

Crucially, Chelsea nipped in at the last minute to sign Willian from under the noses of Spurs, who might argue that was only because of the secret payments.

Image source, Getty Images Image caption, The transfers of David Luiz and Willian were part of the investigation into illegal payments

The investigation found that Chelsea made payments totalling £5.1m between 2012 and 2015 "to provide talent identification services in certain European countries".

This was identified as payments in relation to the registrations of Ramires, Luiz, Schurrle and Matic.

However, by 2016-17 Matic and Luiz were in their second spells at Chelsea . The deal with Benfica which meant Matic and Luiz swapped clubs in 2011 was looked into.

Matic returned to Stamford Bridge in 2014, with Luiz having a spell at Paris St-Germain from 2014 to 2016.

While the deals that took the players back to Chelsea were not specifically referenced, the association was created.

Matic played 35 league games in 2016-17, including 30 in the starting XI. He scored one goal and set up seven.

Only one of those attacking contributions influenced a result, but that was an assist for Chelsea 's first goal in a 2-1 win over Tottenham in November.

Luiz, who was named in the PFA team of the season, started 33 matches and scored one goal - the opener in a 1-1 draw at Liverpool in January.

How Chelsea signed a star team with hidden payments

Published 16 March Chelsea fined but avoid suspended points deduction

Published 31 July Did Chelsea's breaches really impact the title? Tottenham were relentless at the end of the 2016-17 season, winning 12 of their final 13 matches to finish on 86 points.

Yet Antonio Conte's Chelsea were almost as relentless, winning 11 of their last 13 to take the title with 93 points.

Spurs' tally would have been enough for the title in 2015-16, when Leicester finished on 81.

However, since 1999-2000, when Manchester United were champions on 79 points, 86 points would only have won the title twice, including the two most recent seasons.

Tottenham 's problem in 2016-17 was too many draws at the start of the campaign. Despite an unbeaten 11-game start, only five of those were victories.

Chelsea lost more matches - five to Spurs' four - but secured 30 wins to Tottenham 's 26.

Pochettino might argue that the attacking influence from Willian and Hazard proved the difference, with those two players having attacking contributions in eight different matches which led to points.

Then there is the mere aspect of sporting advantage - how the signings of players like Hazard enabled Chelsea to win trophies, qualify for the Champions League and therefore attract more top talent.

Pochettino feels he should have a Premier League title to his name.

Remember that he managed Chelsea for one season, when he struggled to win over supporters.

Chelsea finished sixth in 2023-24, but neither Pochettino nor the club are likely to look back fondly on that period.

It is different at Tottenham , with the Argentine still adored for his five-year spell in charge from 2014.

As well as finishing as Premier League runners-up, he took the club to the Champions League final in 2018-19.

The 86 points earned in 2016-17 is a club record too.

So do Spurs fans share his view?

"Of course I do," said Chris Paouros, co-founder and co-chair of Proud Lilywhites , external and Women of The Lane. , external

"He could tell me the moon was made of halloumi and I'd nod along.

"The Spurs 2016-17 team was the best in the league by most measures: best attack, best defence, fewest defeats, unbeaten at home in the last season of the old White Hart Lane.

"If the playing field was tilted, the least you can do is ask the question."

Paouros knows Spurs will not be handed the title, but said the "rules have to mean something, whoever benefits".

There is another side to this, however.

If you get given a title a decade later because of a rule breach, could you celebrate it?

"It would still be something that Spurs fans would celebrate," said Tristan Foot, secretary of the Tottenham Hotspur Supporters' Trust. "A victory over Chelsea , albeit 10 years after the event."

But that sense of injustice is still there for other Premier League clubs.

"It means that to an extent crime does pay in football," Foot said. "And that's the serious underlying part all of this.

"During the transfer window they were signing players that we had no chance of winning, the obvious example being Willian.

"The Premier League has got to be better about imposing sporting sanctions and making sure that its rules actually have teeth."

With all investigations now concluded, it seems unlikely that Pochettino - or anyone else - will get a retrospective trophy parade.

Will clubs get that same feeling when the Manchester City saga is finally over?

Remember that he managed Chelsea for one season, when he struggled to win over supporters.

Chelsea finished sixth in 2023-24, but neither Pochettino nor the club are likely to look back fondly on that period.

It is different at Tottenham , with the Argentine still adored for his five-year spell in charge from 2014.

As well as finishing as Premier League runners-up, he took the club to the Champions League final in 2018-19.

The 86 points earned in 2016-17 is a club record too.

So do Spurs fans share his view?

"Of course I do," said Chris Paouros, co-founder and co-chair of Proud Lilywhites , external and Women of The Lane. , external

"He could tell me the moon was made of halloumi and I'd nod along.

"The Spurs 2016-17 team was the best in the league by most measures: best attack, best defence, fewest defeats, unbeaten at home in the last season of the old White Hart Lane.

"If the playing field was tilted, the least you can do is ask the question."

Paouros knows Spurs will not be handed the title, but said the "rules have to mean something, whoever benefits".

There is another side to this, however.

If you get given a title a decade later because of a rule breach, could you celebrate it?

"It would still be something that Spurs fans would celebrate," said Tristan Foot, secretary of the Tottenham Hotspur Supporters' Trust. "A victory over Chelsea , albeit 10 years after the event."

But that sense of injustice is still there for other Premier League clubs.

"It means that to an extent crime does pay in football," Foot said. "And that's the serious underlying part all of this.

"During the transfer window they were signing players that we had no chance of winning, the obvious example being Willian.

"The Premier League has got to be better about imposing sporting sanctions and making sure that its rules actually have teeth."

With all investigations now concluded, it seems unlikely that Pochettino - or anyone else - will get a retrospective trophy parade.

Will clubs get that same feeling when the Manchester City saga is finally over?

title: 'My cancer spread while I waited months for surgery': The cost of England's cancer wait times
preview: Cancer care has got worse since the government announced plans to speed up waiting times and save more lives, BBC analysis shows.
summary_raw: Cancer care has got worse since the government announced plans to speed up waiting times and save more lives, BBC analysis shows.
full_text_clean:
Image caption, Alan is one of thousands each month who are not being treated within the cancer target timeframe

Alan was diagnosed with lung cancer after a nodule was found in June last year.

The 70-year-old was meant to be operated on within weeks but ended up waiting nearly five months, by which time the cancer had spread, making his surgery more complex.

"I was so frustrated and angry and couldn't understand why they would leave me like that," says Alan.

On two occasions, scans were cancelled because machines had broken and for weeks he heard little or nothing from the hospital about when he would eventually have the urgent surgery.

Alan is one of thousands each month in England who are not being treated within the target timeframe.

Earlier this year, the government's National Cancer Plan, along with the NHS Planning Guidance, set out that 80% of patients in England would start treatment within 62 days from urgent GP referral by March 2027. This was to reach 85% by March 2029.

But in the months since the government announced this ambition, performance has got worse, according to NHS England data, not better.

Now, 71.2% of patients start cancer treatment within the 62 day timeframe. Previously it was 71.9%.

Prof Pat Price, a leading UK clinical academic oncologist, says the government targets "are now simply impossible to hit", after what she describes as a "complete loss of momentum".

Price attributes the current failures to a "complete lack of a plan or accountability".

The plan stated that a new independent cancer board would be established, but it is still not known who will be leading this group.

NHS data released on Thursday, for July, reveals 10 out of 120 hospital trusts in England managed to get 85% of patients to start treatment within 62 of their urgent referral by a GP.

Radiotherapy UK analysis, shared exclusively with the BBC, suggests more than 2,800 extra patients would need to start treatment every month - a near 15% increase on current numbers - to achieve the March 2027 target.

That is likely to grow as referrals keep rising across nearly every cancer type.

Price says thousands of patients "are going to die unnecessarily, just because the government can't get their act together to treat people on time".

For every month a cancer patient waits before starting treatment, their chance of survival falls by around 10%, on average.

By the time Alan had his operation, the cancer had spread to his lymph nodes and the nodule "had grown at an alarming rate", according to the lung specialist.

He has since been told the cancer has cleared awaiting his one-year review, but the operation has left him in debilitating pain. "I used to play golf and get out and about. Now I can't do any of the things I love," says Alan.

Roughly 54,000 more patients will need to start treatment within 62 days before 2029 for the government to hit its goal.

One NHS trust that is gaining traction on its waiting list numbers is Salisbury, but it is still not hitting targets.

Staff say there is no single fix, just a relentless focus on getting the basics right; making sure patients know about their appointments and turn up, keeping IT systems working, recruiting the right people, making sure surgical lists are full and expanding capacity.

Much of the visible progress has come through skin and prostate cancer, two of the most common cancers in the country.

Diane had a cancerous lump removed from her face at Salisbury District Hospital a few weeks ago, using an innovative procedure, which checks tumour margins are clear while the patient is still in surgery.

That means no follow-up operations, and it allows for complex reconstruction that leaves hardly a trace.

"It's amazing, you literally can't see I had a large cancerous lesion removed from my cheek," she tells the BBC in the waiting room.

Consultant plastic surgeon Neil Wickham checked her face, confirmed a biopsied lump on her arm was benign, and referred her to ENT for a separate lump in her neck.

It is the kind of joined-up care the government's Cancer Plan was meant to trigger in cancer units across England.

Image caption, Diane benefited from an innovative procedure when she had a cancerous lump removed from her face

But over in pathology at the Salisbury trust, head of department Lee Phillips is feeling the pressure. His histology lab receives cancer service biopsies from across the hospital for diagnosis.

"The sheer volume of specimens we have coming in is our problem," he says.

"We need more staff and more kit if we're going to keep up with demand," Phillips says.

Radiotherapy is another bottleneck crying out for staff and kit. Like many trusts, Salisbury has no machine on site, so patients needing daily sessions over one to three weeks must travel up to an hour to Southampton, and sometimes Bath.

But staff in Salisbury also say missed appointments, whether down to late letters, illness, transport problems or anxiety, are a constant drain on a system already stretched thin.

Emilia Scutt, cancer manager in Salisbury, says that efforts to reduce missed appointments have really helped their numbers.

"We know cancer can be terrifying so we are a bit like a dog with the bone, backing up patients and supporting them wherever we can."

Trusts with the sharpest declines in performance - including Buckinghamshire Healthcare, Bolton NHS Foundation Trust, Royal Devon University Healthcare Trust, East Cheshire, and Torbay and South Devon - told the BBC they face pressures across the board. Rising demand, workforce shortages and diagnostic bottlenecks have all played a part.

Some pointed to industrial action and staff sickness, others to reliance on outside diagnostic providers or major changes to how their systems work. All say they are investing in extra capacity, working through backlogs and redesigning pathways, and are already seeing early signs of improvement.

"If government is serious about delivering on the ambitions of the National Cancer Plan for England, it must match ambition with urgency," said Steve Haines of Macmillan Cancer Support.

He said that "visible progress" was needed on a promise to set up a National Cancer Board to oversee progress on improving waiting times and treatment.

A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson says "cancer waiting times are moving in the right direction will all three cancer standards better than a year ago".

They concede that "there is more to do," and that the plan "will help people get diagnosed earlier and begin treatment sooner."

Additional reporting Daniel Wainwright and Jess Carr

title: Five killed and 67 injured in Russian strike on shopping centre, Ukraine says
preview: The attack in Pavlohrad city centre was the third Russian strike on a mall within days, local media report.
summary_raw: The attack in Pavlohrad city centre was the third Russian strike on a mall within days, local media report.
full_text_clean:
Image source, State Emergency Service of Ukraine By Patrick Jackson Published 10 September 2026 Ukrainian officials say five people were killed and 67 others were wounded when a Russian drone hit a shopping mall in Pavlohrad, a city in Dnipropetrovsk region.

Shops and vehicles were hit in the daylight attack which took place "when the streets were full of people", Interior Minister Ivan Vyhivskyi said.

Two other shopping malls - in the cities of Zaporizhzhia and Sumy - were targeted by Russian air strikes earlier this week, according to Ukrainian media.

Russia reported a Ukrainian seaborne drone attack on the resort city of Sochi overnight on Wednesday, in which 28 people were wounded, as well as three more deaths blamed on Ukrainian attacks.

A full-scale war has been raging between Russia and Ukraine since Russian President Vladimir Putin launched an invasion more than four and a half years ago.

A new peacemaking effort by envoys sent by US President Donald Trump at the weekend appears to have yielded few concrete results, after talks in Moscow with Putin and in Kyiv with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.

Russia's new jet-powered drones outpacing Ukraine's air defences with daily launches

Published 19 hours ago Peace talks rich in symbolism but fundamental differences between Russia and Ukraine remain

Published 4 days ago Two die at Moldovan border as Russia-Ukraine drone war rages

Published 1 day ago Kyiv air raid alerts at record high as Russia launches round-the-clock strikes

Published 3 days ago Rescuers dig through Ukraine mall wreckage as Zelensky condemns 'despicable' Russian strike

Published 22 August Images released by the State Emergency Service of Ukraine show firefighters directing water hoses at burning vehicles amid clouds of smoke on a street in Pavlohrad.

In a Telegram post, regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha said of the 67 people injured, eight are children.

Zelensky offered his condolences to the families and loved ones of those killed in Thursday's attack.

"The Russians used drones to kill people who were simply standing near shopping centres," Ukraine's president said in his statement.

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha called the drone attack a "tactic of coercion". "Russia believes that relentless attacks on civilians can exhaust Ukrainians and force Ukraine into concession," he said.

Pavlohrad, a logistics hub near the central city of Dnipro, has come under heavy attack previously, with two people killed in an attack on warehouses there last month.

Ukrainian officials say a Russian drone attack on a mall in Sumy on Wednesday killed two people and wounded 20. On Thursday, Russian aerial bombing reportedly injured eight people in Sumy, including three children.

In Zaporizhzhia, capital of the region of the same name which was partially annexed by Russia soon after the invasion, a shopping mall was almost completely destroyed on Monday, its owners reported.

However, it was closed at the time and there were no immediate reports of casualties.

One of the bloodiest attacks on a shopping centre came last month, when Ukrainian officials say Russian drones killed at least 16 people and injured 130 in the city of Kryvyi Rih.

Shopping malls in Russian-controlled parts of Ukraine have also come under attack, with a Ukrainian drone attack reported on Monday on a mall in the port city of Mariupol, Donetsk region, and another attack on the city of Donetsk last month.

On Wednesday night, a number of Ukrainian seaborne drones attacked the shoreline at Sochi, Russian officials say. Two of the 28 people reported injured are children.

On Thursday, Russian officials reported that a Ukrainian drone strike on the town of Novy Oskol in Belgord Region had killed one person and wounded six others.

It was further announced that a Ukrainian attack on a car in Russian-controlled Zaporizhzhia on Wednesday had killed a girl of 15, also injuring a child of six and two women; and a separate attack on a civilian lorry in the same region had killed a man.

title: US airport security weighs major changes 25 years after 9/11
preview: Americans will soon be able to see their loved ones off at airport gates as part of the changes.
summary_raw: Americans will soon be able to see their loved ones off at airport gates as part of the changes.
full_text_clean:
Image source, Getty Images By Ana Faguy Published 4 hours ago Americans will soon be able to see their loved ones off at airport gates, restoring airport policies that were put in place in the wake of 9/11.

The Transportation Security Administration (TSA) announced that it will soon allow individuals without tickets to pass through security and go to airport gates with loved ones.

TSA is also considering allowing some US passengers to take full water bottles through security, reversing a policy that was implemented after a foiled 2006 terror plot.

The changes represent some of the biggest shifts in aviation security in decades and likely stem from improved technology rather than a decline in standards, an aviation expert told the BBC.

Americans who participate in TSA PreCheck or have a known traveller number will be the first to take advantage of the new policies. Those travellers already go through a pre-approval process with the US government in order to receive speedier security screening at US airports.

Individuals who have TSA PreCheck and want to go to an airport gate without a ticket can apply online one to three days before their planned visits.

TSA announced this week that the Gateside TSA PreCheck programme will be offered at 13 airports across the US.

"This new program makes it easier to return to the gate for welcomes and send-offs, meet friends during a layover, and enjoy dining and shopping along the way, bringing back the moments that once defined air travel," TSA wrote on its website.

Jeff Price, an aviation security expert and professor at Metro State University Denver, told the BBC that the post-9/11 policy change was about reducing the number of people security officers had to screen.

"It keeps the lines moving and allows us to focus more on the traveling passenger," he said.

But now improvements in technology mean these policies can change, he said.

In addition to reinstating gate visitors, the Trump administration is also looking at allowing passengers with TSA PreCheck to take water with them through airport security, according to US media reports.

That would reverse a ban put in place following attempted terrorist attacks in the UK in 2006, in which individuals planned to smuggle liquid chemical mixtures inside soft drink and sports drink bottles.

The BBC requested confirmation of this reported change; TSA did not respond.

Price said newer security machines that TSA is installing to replace traditional X-ray machines have computed tomography capabilities, which "can do a much better job of detecting liquid-based explosives".

These updates to security protocols follow a move from TSA last year to end the requirement that passengers remove their shoes during security screenings, an unpopular policy in place for two decades.

Reaction to the announcements on social media was mixed. Some older users who remember a time before these policies praised a return to normalcy, while younger users questioned whether the changes signaled any decline in safety.

"People have a nostalgia for a pre 9/11, it's a calling back to a normal world, and I can see that part of it," Price said. "I can see people wanting to get back to something that they feel more comfortable with, which was a pre 9/11 world."

But Price said these changes will not impact the safety of passengers as long as core security measures remain in place and standards continue to be high.

"I don't want to compromise [valid security measures] simply for a nostalgic feeling before 9/11," he said. "I don't think we should make those types of decisions so that we feel better. We can make those types of decisions as long as the security measures are not compromised, and that's always what I look for in these situations."

Drone display recreates the Twin Towers over New York City

US airports lift shoe removal requirement at security screenings

title: Teacher sexually abused pupils at multiple schools
preview: Bronwen James, 30, admitted abusing two girls and was convicted of offences against a teenage boy.
summary_raw: Bronwen James, 30, admitted abusing two girls and was convicted of offences against a teenage boy.
full_text_clean:
Image source, PA Media Image caption, Bronwen James pleaded guilty to nine offences and was found guilty of a further three after a trial at Winchester Crown Court

A teacher has been found guilty of sexually abusing a 16-year-old boy after previously admitting offences against two teenage girls.

Former PE teacher Bronwen James, 30, of Chippenham, Wiltshire, admitted nine sexual offences against two teenage girls - one a pupil at Bitterne Park School in Southampton and the other at Hardenhuish School in Chippenham.

She was convicted earlier at Winchester Crown Court of three counts of sexual activity with a 16-year-old boy who also attended Bitterne Park School.

During the trial the prosecution said James "craved" attention and "abused the trust put in her" as a teacher .

The jury found James guilty of the three counts of sexual activity with a child by a person in a position of trust by a majority of 11 to one and acquitted her of a fourth charge.

Due to legal restrictions covering the trial, media had been unable to report James' guilty pleas against two girls - which she made in January - and the jury were not told about them until after they had passed their verdict.

Image source, PA Media Image caption, James was told she would go to prison on Monday ahead of her sentencing

James showed no emotion as the verdict was read out and stood looking at the floor as the jury left the courtroom.

She was told by the judge she must surrender her passport and would be monitored with an electronic tag until Monday, when she will be taken to prison ahead of her sentencing.

During the five-day trial, prosecutors said James had entered into a "flirty" relationship with the pupil and they had communicated via Snapchat before they had sex at her house "three or four" times.

The jury also heard that James told the boy she loved him and wanted him to move away with her.

Giving evidence in court, the teenager said: "I thought she cared about me.

"I thought this was great, any teenage boy's dream, but [now] I think it was wrong. At the time I wasn't thinking that."

James denied all charges, alleging that the boy had made them up to "look cool" .

The nine offences against two teenage girls include six counts of engaging in sexual activity with a child, two counts of engaging in sexual communication with a child and one count of making indecent images of a child.

"Bronwen James was trusted to educate and protect children - instead, she used that trust to groom and sexually abuse three students," said senior crown prosecutor Bethany Adams.

Image caption, Adams said James had shown a "sustained pattern of predatory behaviour"

"James manipulated her victims with calculated precision, exploiting her position of authority to isolate them and normalise the abuse," she added.

"This was not a lapse in judgement; it was a sustained pattern of predatory behaviour against children in her care."

A spokesperson from the NSPCC said James had "exploited" a "position of trust" where she was supposed to "support, protect and educate those in her professional care".

"When someone in authority abuses a trusted relationship, young people can find it particularly difficult to recognise what is happening or to speak out about it, and it can have a profound and lasting impact on their wellbeing," they added.

A spokesperson from Hardenhuish School said they "commend" the courage of the young people who came forward to give evidence in the case.

"The safety and wellbeing of our pupils is, and always will be, our highest priority," they said.

title: Father of A66 teen charged with funeral assault
preview: Police charged Gye Worthy with assault at the funeral for his son who was killed in the A66 crash.
summary_raw: Police charged Gye Worthy with assault at the funeral for his son who was killed in the A66 crash.
full_text_clean:
Image source, Social media Image caption, Cole Robert Worthy, on the right, was one of seven killed in a head-on crash with a police car

The father of one of the five men who were killed in a wrong-way crash with a police car has been charged with assaulting someone at his son's funeral.

Gye Worthy, 39, was arrested at Teesside Crematorium in Middlesbrough following a disturbance during the service on Wednesday.

His son Cole Worthy, 17, died when the Volkswagon Passat he and four others were in collided with a marked armed police car on the A66 in South Bank in the early hours of 22 August.

Cleveland Police said Gye Worthy has been charged with common assault and obstructing police and is due to appear at Teesside Magistrates' Court in October.

Cole Worthy's funeral was held on the same day as that of PC Matthew Blades, 37, who was one of the officers killed in the crash.

PC Blades had been travelling along the A66 with his colleague PC Tom Clough when their car was struck head-on by the Passat travelling in the wrong direction.

The pair were in a vehicle looking for the Passat after its cloned registration plates triggered a camera, although they were not involved in the pursuit which preceded the crash, according to the Independent Office for Police Conduct.

Image source, PA Image caption, Prior to the A66 crash a home linked to the Worthy family had been rammed

The others killed in the Passat were Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jakub Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, and 17-year-old Theo Rae.

It later emerged a property on a street in Acklam, Middlesbrough, linked to the Worthy family had been rammed by a car shortly before the fatal crash.

title: Ex-Tory campaign chief pleads guilty over election bet
preview: Anthony Lee passed confidential information to his wife Laura Lee about when the 2024 election would be held.
summary_raw: Anthony Lee passed confidential information to his wife Laura Lee about when the 2024 election would be held.
full_text_clean:
Image caption, Anthony Lee and his wife Laura pleaded guilty at Southwark Crown Court on Thursday

The Conservatives' former director of campaigning and his wife have pleaded guilty to cheating at gambling by placing bets on the date of the 2024 general election.

Anthony Lee stood to win approximately £15,000 after placing more than 60 successful bets totalling £1,549, the Gambling Commission said.

He passed confidential information to his wife about when former Prime Minister Rishi Sunak was planning to call the general election.

Laura Lee, who was a parliamentary candidate at the time, placed eight successful bets on the election date totalling £535 and would have profited by around £5,000.

On Thursday at Southwark Crown Court, Anthony Lee pleaded guilty to two offences and Laura Lee pleaded guilty to one offence.

They will be sentenced in October.

The trials of 10 other defendants will take place in September 2027 and January 2028.

Former MP Craig Williams, who was Sunak's closest parliamentary aide at the time, pleaded guilty in June and will be sentenced at a later date.

In Williams' case, the prosecution said he bet £250, £100, and £22.50 on the date of the 2024 election, telling the court he "used highly sensitive and confidential information".

When details of the scandal first emerged in June 2024, Williams admitted making a "huge error of judgment".

Sunak's decision to call the poll was a surprise to many, including many Conservative MPs, who were expecting an autumn date.

The Conservative Party has been approached for comment.

title: Two goals in two games - Sesko gives Man Utd a different threat
preview: Benjamin Sesko's return to Manchester United's starting line-up is well timed ahead of Sunday's Premier League encounter with Manchester City
summary_raw: Benjamin Sesko's return to Manchester United's starting line-up is well timed ahead of Sunday's Premier League encounter with Manchester City
full_text_clean:
Man United put four past Sabah on Champions League return

Manchester United reporter at Old Trafford Published 1 hour ago Manchester United will experience far stiffer tests of their Champions League credentials than Sabah FK gave them at Old Trafford.

In fact, it would be no surprise if the Azerbaijani champions were by some distance the weakest of the eight league stage opponents Michael Carrick's side will come up against.

However, there were some important lessons for head coach Carrick to absorb.

The biggest of them is that United are a much more effective unit when Benjamin Sesko starts.

This was the first time the Slovenian had done that since the Liverpool game last March, when he finally accepted he could no longer play through the shin issue that had been plaguing him for a number of weeks.

It had been hoped Sesko would be fit for the start of the Premier League season.

As it turned out, he was only at the stage where he could be brought on as a substitute in the second half of the opening-day trip to Hull. The same also applied for the subsequent outings against Ipswich and Everton .

It was Sabah's bad luck that Sesko was fit to start against them – and it showed.

At 6ft 5in, the 23-year-old has a physical presence United's other strikers lack.

Amad Diallo's current absence has robbed Carrick of the option to start Bryan Mbeumo at the head of his attack, as he did during pre-season, but Matheus Cunha is not without ability in that role.

The problem is that the Brazilian likes to drift and drop back into space, which leaves a gap at the apex of Manchester United 's attack.

Sesko offers a totally different threat. He pushes defences back. He is not easy to dispossess. He runs at opponents rather than away from them.

At Everton , it was his size that allowed him to convert a close-range header that looked set to give United victory but ultimately didn't, because of Ainsley Maitland-Niles' stunning late strike.

Against Sabah FK, Sesko had threatened with an impudent first-half back-flick before Mbeumo sent him running beyond the visitors' defence.

Sesko had clarity of thought, swiftly moving the ball past goalkeeper Stas Pokatilov before steering the ball into an empty net.

Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Sesko has now scored 12 goals in his past 21 games for Manchester United

"Of course, I'm happy with my goal," Sesko told TNT after the game.

"I saw him rushing out, and it was a great opportunity to take the ball away from him and make the goal a little bit easier."

United's scenario is not that Mbeumo and Cunha can't do that, it is more that Sesko can do it in addition to presenting the physical threat.

'Good control for a big man' is one of football's oldest cliches. Yet the players who can combine size with skill and pace are exceptionally useful.

"He definitely offers a different kind of threat," said Carrick.

"That's the beauty of it, really. We know what Ben gives us. There's not many around that kind of give you what Ben does in terms of his physique, his physicality, playing on the last line and his speed to run in behind. He's a real threat.

"It's great to have him back at this level after working to get his fitness back.

"A couple of goals and good performances, and good minutes in him. I'm really pleased with the way he's gone."

'Such a gamble' leaving Fernandes on for 90 minutes

It is a fairly obvious thing to say but Carrick now has a big decision before Sunday's Premier League derby with Manchester City at Old Trafford.

Does he trust Sesko's fitness and stick with him? Or does he revert to Cunha, given there has been no indication Amad is ready to return.

On this evidence, Sesko should get the nod. That in turn would leave Carrick to decide whether Cunha, who opened the scoring against Sabah, or Marcus Rashford, who was an unused substitute, should start on the left.

Rashford has yet to score a goal or create one since he returned to his boyhood club after last season's loan spell at Barcelona.

However, he has been their most consistent threat with his pace and direct running.

Cunha drifts into similar positions to skipper Bruno Fernandes, and Carrick may decide United's structure works better with England international Rashford.

If that is the case, he wasn't admitting it on a night when Fernandes also scored.

Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Matheus Cunha (right) and skipper Bruno Fernandes were both on target for Manchester United in their Champions League victory over Sabah FK

"It's not an easy decision, of course it's not," Carrick said of his team selection.

"But it's definitely one I'd prefer: to have goals in the team and for the boys to be playing well.

"The understanding they all have is that sometimes it's going to be a start, sometimes it's going to be finishing the game. We need that within the group, from game to game over the season, to be able to call upon slightly different kind of things at different times.

"It's fantastic they're all in good form and started so well."

Fernandes finished off a brilliant move to double United's lead

title: England's push for two-day win halted by weather
preview: England's charge towards a two-day victory in the final Test against Pakistan is only halted by rain at Edgbaston.
summary_raw: England's charge towards a two-day victory in the final Test against Pakistan is only halted by rain at Edgbaston.
full_text_clean:
England in complete control against Pakistan in dominant day two

Cricket Correspondent at Edgbaston Published 10 September 2026 Third Rothesay Test, Edgbaston (day two of five)

Pakistan 133 (Shakeel 43; Tongue 4-42) & 52-2 (Robinson 2-10)

England 453 (Brook 75, Smith 69, Lawrence 65, Gay 60, Robinson 50; Razaullah 4-148)

England's charge towards a two-day win in the final Test against Pakistan was only halted by rain at Edgbaston.

The tourists were battling for survival on 52-2 - 268 adrift of making England bat again - when the bad weather intervened for a second and final occasion in Birmingham.

The time was 17:07 BST. With the possibility of an extra half an hour available to force a result, play could have continued until 19:00 if conditions had allowed.

Given the fragility of the Pakistan batting - the tourists have not reached 200 or batted for more than 51 overs in the series - there was a real possibility England would earn victory inside two days after Ollie Robinson reduced the visitors to 0-2.

Instead, the players will return on Friday, when England will complete a 3-0 series clean sweep.

The eventual outcome of this match was barely in doubt when England began Thursday on 156-4, leading by 23.

Contributions of 75 from Harry Brook, 69 by Jamie Smith, 65 scored by Dan Lawrence and 50 from Robinson pushed England to 453, a huge first-innings lead of 320.

The only disappointment was that no England batter pushed on to make a century, meaning Ben Duckett's ton against New Zealand at Trent Bridge will remain the home side's only hundred of the summer.

Dominant England set target for Pakistan at Edgbaston

Smith racks up England's fourth half-century of the innings

One of the criticisms of the previous England regime, under captain Ben Stokes and coach Brendon McCullum, was their inability to finish series strongly.

England have lost the final Test in each of their past six series. Some of their worst performances in the Bazball era came in dead rubbers after a series had been won, notably at home to Sri Lanka in 2024 and away to New Zealand later the same year.

Stokes often said he did not like the word "ruthless" and there were plenty of times his side lacked ruthlessness. On this occasion, Root's England are showing their ruthless side.

The quality of the opposition should be taken into account - Stokes' England would have comfortably beaten this poor Pakistan side. The hosts also had the better of the conditions on Thursday, batting under blue sky then bowling when it got dark overhead.

But, under Root, England are showing a new-found calmness, along with a willingness to find the right tempo to their batting. The way they extended their lead on the second day was an example of a more mature approach.

And, in Robinson, they have a bowler in the form of his life, a purple patch England will hope carries through the winter and to next summer's Ashes.

Lawrence races to 50 in a strong morning session

title: England captain Jones calls for fertility support
preview: England captain Meg Jones wants the Red Roses to have access to fertility support and egg freezing.
summary_raw: England captain Meg Jones wants the Red Roses to have access to fertility support and egg freezing.
full_text_clean:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Meg Jones took over the England captaincy in March

Rugby union commentator Published 2 hours ago Meg Jones, captain of the England women's rugby union team, wants Red Roses players to have access to fertility support and egg freezing.

Speaking to BBC Sport, Jones said: "Why should my opportunity to have a family be taken away from me because I want to pursue my career?"

Jones revealed she has already started her fertility journey with her fiancee after visiting a clinic to have their egg count checked.

The 29-year-old says that she's an "open book" on some subjects and wants to "share her journey" as she discusses both her upcoming wedding and family planning with equal comfort.

"We were looking to freeze, but actually the advice was we don't need to freeze yet so we can probably wait till after the wedding," said Jones. "That's where we were going to look to conceive."

The Red Roses are considered to have one of the best maternity policies in international women's sport, with two World Cup winners having recently given birth and two more expecting.

When approached about providing fertility packages for England players, a Rugby Football Union (RFU) spokesperson said: "We work hard to support players in the decisions they make around fertility and family planning and are proud to have been at the forefront of industry-leading support in this area.

"We already have comprehensive maternity and parental policies in place and are always open to exploring how that support can evolve."

While there is no specific policy around financial compensation for fertility treatment for England players, it is understood there are ongoing discussions at the RFU and it could be introduced in the future.

Players are currently entitled to a week of paid leave per treatment cycle for treatment and appointments.

Jones first said that the Red Roses should "jump on that" policy while on the "The Good, The Scaz & The Rugby" podcast when discussing the Spanish football federation's announcement , external that it would pay for its international women's players to freeze their eggs

In August, Chelsea women also unveiled a partnership , external with a fertility company to provide workshops, treatments, counselling and assessments to support their players.

It was revealed in The Observer , external that the fund set up by Chelsea would cover the cost of the whole squad freezing their eggs.

Speaking before England's match with Australia on Saturday, Jones told BBC Sport: "I wouldn't have thought it was something that we were lacking from maybe a governing point of view, but now I think about it I'm like, yeah, actually, I haven't got that opportunity to go and create a family and be guided on.

"It's definitely been flagged with our group. Again, you learn so much from other teams… and I think the more we can empower women the better for the game as a whole, and better for women in general."

title: 2030 Winter Olympics boss departs amid turmoil
preview: Edgar Grospiron leaves his position as president of the organising committee for the 2030 French Alps Winter Olympics just 18 months after his appointment.
summary_raw: Edgar Grospiron leaves his position as president of the organising committee for the 2030 French Alps Winter Olympics just 18 months after his appointment.
full_text_clean:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Freestyle skier Grospiron is a two-time Olympic medallist and three-time former world champion

Edgar Grospiron has left his position as president of the organising committee for the 2030 French Alps Winter Olympics just 18 months after his appointment.

The departure of Grospiron, the 1992 Olympic moguls champion, was confirmed at a meeting of the committee's executive board on Thursday, marking the latest setback in the event's troubled governance.

In a statement, the organising committee said: "His decision to leave the presidency is part of a deliberate, organised and fully assumed transition, taken in the interests of the project and its governance.

"It reflects a shared desire with stakeholders to enable the organisation to quickly enter this new operational phase."

Confirming his departure via a post on LinkedIn, Grospiron said his decision followed "months of tension".

"I draw the conclusion that the conditions are not met for me to continue this," he wrote.

Grospiron's tenure, which began in February 2025, has been plagued by internal turmoil and logistical challenges.

In February 2026, chief executive officer Cyril Linette left the committee, citing "insurmountable disagreements" with Grospiron.

Linette's departure followed a number of other high-profile resignations, including chief operating officer Anne Murac and communications director Arthur Richer.

Budget cuts have plagued the planning process, with Grospiron admitting in February they had "little time, little money".

However, he remained confident he could "deliver a Games that will honour our vision and ambition" provided there was "serenity" and "continuity" from the organising committee.

In May, the committee was forced to shelve the Games' 'ice sports hub' in Nice after the city's mayor, Eric Ciotti, refused to allow OGC Nice's Allianz Riviera Stadium to be converted into a temporary ice rink.

The ice events will now be hosted in Lyon, with the exception of speed skating, which will take place in Heerenveen in the Netherlands.

Two months later, following a tense board meeting in July, French Olympic Committee president Amelie Oudea-Castera told La Tribune Dimanche , external that they were "once again facing governance problems".

Despite another departure from the organising committee, French sports minister Marina Ferrari says there is "no concern about what comes next".

"The bid is continuing to move forward," she told reporters. "Our teams are mobilised and working. We are confident about the future of the Alpes project."

The International Olympic Committee praised Grospiron's "crucial work in laying the foundations for the success" of the Games.

"The IOC will continue working in close collaboration with the organising committee to build on the solid foundations that Mr Grospiron has laid," the statement added.

title: Hamilton and Leclerc 'squash' Monza controversy
preview: Lewis Hamilton says he and Ferrari team-mate Charles Leclerc have "squashed" any controversy between them from the Italian Grand Prix.
summary_raw: Lewis Hamilton says he and Ferrari team-mate Charles Leclerc have "squashed" any controversy between them from the Italian Grand Prix.
full_text_clean:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Lewis Hamilton lost places at the beginning of the Italian Grand Prix following his battle with team-mate Charles Leclerc

F1 correspondent in Madrid Published 6 hours ago Lewis Hamilton says he and Ferrari team-mate Charles Leclerc have "squashed" any controversy between them after a difficult Italian Grand Prix.

Leclerc forced Hamilton into the gravel at the first chicane at Monza on Sunday, and then crashed two laps later. Hamilton recovered to finish a disappointed sixth.

It was the second flashpoint between the Ferrari drivers in two races, after an argument over the radio during the Dutch Grand Prix when Leclerc resisted a request to move aside for Hamilton.

Hamilton said: "What's great is that there was no shying away from having a discussion. We sat face to face, just him and I, and talked about it.

"We were just both open and honest, and we squashed it. We can move on. I think that one shows the maturity from him."

Speaking at the media day for this weekend's Spanish Grand Prix, the seven-time champion added: "It's healthy. It's a relationship we have built over time. Of course, there's going to be frustrations and I'm sure there'll be more times where we're close because we're very close in pace.

"We both want to win just as much as each other, and we both want to do well for the team as well."

'It started as a joke, a fantasy' - F1 heads to football-obsessed Madrid

Published 18 hours ago How to follow Spanish Grand Prix on the BBC

Published 12 hours ago Leclerc said: "It's kind of clear that we never want to see a car of the same team in the grass.

"After reviewing, we spoke with Lewis. I obviously know I went too far in turn two and I said it to Lewis and I think it's very clear what we should do or should avoid going forward.

"But I won't go into much more details of what we've said. The only thing I can say is that it definitely did not affect the good relationship that we have and it will not affect anything going forward. And that is the most important for me, really.

"I know we are driving for Ferrari and if there's one race where you don't want that to happen, it's in Monza and when these things happen at our home race, then it does a huge mess outside.

"However, looking at the race from outside, there's been also some friction between other team-mates and the only thing we end up speaking of is Lewis and me, which I don't think is quite right. But that doesn't mean we did everything perfect."

Hamilton acknowledged again that Ferrari had to improve their operations, after three consecutive race weekends where qualifying has not gone to plan.

"It's really just making sure we're executing to make sure we get the best result for the team," he said. "Instead of us working against each other and finish fourth and fifth, maybe we can work together and get a podium and pull off more points.

"It's a longer term process. It's not something we can just change into this weekend. There's a huge amount of moving parts, there's a lot of people, there's a culture that's been there for a long, long time and moving big pieces is not so easy."

How the 'Monumental' turn became the signature section of the new Madring F1 circuit in Madrid

F1 faces a fresh challenge this weekend at the first Spanish Grand at the new Madring, a hybrid street circuit built on the Ifema complex near the city's international airport.

Hamilton said: "It's a massively challenging circuit. Of all the new tracks that I've gone to, this one, maybe Saudi, are the two closest in terms of how difficult it was to get on top of the car and find the right lines and such."

Mercedes driver George Russell said: "It's a crazy circuit, I would put it. Arguably one of the most risky circuits of the whole calendar.

"Because you have real high-speed corners, sort of Jeddah-esque, the walls are very close, so there's no margin for error, but then you have other corners... where you're coming from a high speed into a slow braking zone, you're braking and turning at the same time, so locking tyres are going to be easy and if you lock up you'll be straight in the wall.

"So, excited to try that out, I think it's going to be really challenging for us as drivers, the race is going to be challenging to overtake, so on the whole it's not an easy one."

Russell heads into the race 66 points behind team-mate Kimi Antonelli after the Italian's landmark victory in Monza from 19th on the grid.

The Briton acknowledged that his title hopes with nine or 10 races left, amid uncertainty about the end of the season, were fading fast.

"I would definitely need some luck and I need some good performances," Russell said. "It's not really something I'm thinking about, because he's performing better than me, so he deserves to be leading the championship.

"There's still a long way to go, but he's yet to have a bad weekend in terms of performance.

"So he's performing exceptionally well, my performances are better, but if I want to win this championship, I'm going to need some luck on the way. But it's not something I'm focused on. I'm focused on driving faster and just finding more performance."

Antonelli said: "I don't really want to try thinking about the championship. I think Monza was the proof that I wasn't driving thinking about, or worrying about the championship. I was just driving to win, to do my best. So that's the mindset."

The Italian said his win in Monza was "so far the best day of my life and definitely one I will remember forever".

He said a day karting with Mercedes on Monday helped him move on from the excitement of the day before.

"After Monza, that night, that day overall, I was very excited. But then going karting on Monday helped me to go back to earth, just go back to the ground.

"It was a good day, good fun day with the team. It was also a way to remind myself where I came from, all the journey that was done.

"And then about pressure, I try to embrace it as much as possible. And I try to see it as a positive thing and try to see it as an opportunity too. That's also what is helping me to stay calm under difficult situations."

F1 faces a fresh challenge this weekend at the first Spanish Grand at the new Madring, a hybrid street circuit built on the Ifema complex near the city's international airport.

"So he's performing exceptionally well, my performances are better, but if I want to win this championship, I'm going to need some luck on the way. But it's not something I'm focused on. I'm focused on driving faster and just finding more performance."

The Italian said his win in Monza was "so far the best day of my life and definitely one I will remember forever".

He said a day karting with Mercedes on Monday helped him move on from the excitement of the day before.

"After Monza, that night, that day overall, I was very excited. But then going karting on Monday helped me to go back to earth, just go back to the ground.

"It was a good day, good fun day with the team. It was also a way to remind myself where I came from, all the journey that was done.

"And then about pressure, I try to embrace it as much as possible. And I try to see it as a positive thing and try to see it as an opportunity too. That's also what is helping me to stay calm under difficult situations."
